excerpt: A 2,000 sq ft suite with two single-user restrooms pays nearly double per fixture for descaling compared with a 30,000 sq ft building with eight core restrooms. Here is why minimums, production rates, and equipment choices create that gap, and how small and large tenants can each negotiate a fair unit price.
quickAnswer: Small suites under 2,500 sq ft usually hit the $110–$190 descaling project minimum, which works out to $28–$48 per fixture when only four fixtures are serviced. Buildings over 25,000 sq ft with 50 or more fixtures typically pay $14–$24 per fixture because technicians descale four or more fixtures per hour in a continuous route. Routine service stays near $15–$30 per restroom per visit in both cases, but large buildings negotiate toward the low end.

blocks.text: Why Restroom Unit Prices Shrink as Buildings Grow

Restroom sanitization and descaling look like simple per-fixture work, but the economics behave very differently at the two ends of the market. A small professional suite of around 2,000 sq ft typically has two single-user restrooms, each with one toilet and one sink. A 30,000 sq ft multi-floor building may have eight core restrooms with 56 fixtures between them. The labor per fixture is similar, yet the per-fixture invoice is not, because three fixed costs are spread over very different volumes: mobilization and travel, chemical and PPE setup, and the vendor's minimum charge.

Understanding where your building sits on that curve tells you which pricing lever to push. Small tenants should negotiate bundling and minimum relief. Large tenants should negotiate production-rate pricing and push routine per-restroom rates to the bottom of the national band.

headers: Routine rate per restroom per visit

blocks.text: In a 2,000 sq ft suite, descaling four fixtures takes a technician a little over an hour. At $55–$95 per specialty hour, that labor is worth $66–$114, but nearly every vendor sets a project minimum around $110–$190 to cover the drive, chemical kit, and PPE. The result is an effective $28–$48 per fixture, roughly double the large-building rate. The same dynamic hits routine service: the base janitorial bracket for spaces under 2,500 sq ft is $0.12–$0.20 per sq ft per visit, and the $90–$135 per-visit minimum often overrides the formula entirely.

items: Bundle descaling into a scheduled routine visit so the vendor avoids a second trip; many will waive the project minimum when the technician is already on site.
Coordinate with neighboring suites on the same floor to share one descaling work order and split mobilization.
Shift from quarterly to semiannual descaling if traffic is under 25 users per restroom per day, cutting minimum charges in half.
Ask for a flat annual restroom fee rather than per-event pricing to smooth minimum charges across 12 months.

blocks.title: Small-office negotiating line
blocks.text: Ask the vendor: if descaling is performed during a regularly scheduled visit, what is the per-fixture rate with no separate minimum? Most will quote $18–$25 per fixture, saving a two-restroom suite $40–$90 per event.

In a 30,000 sq ft building, a two-person crew can stage chemicals once per floor, descale toilets and urinals in sequence while acid dwell times overlap, and flush drains in bulk. Production climbs to four or more fixtures per technician hour, so 56 fixtures take about 14 hours. At $55–$95 per hour, the job lands at $770–$1,330, or $14–$24 per fixture. The base janitorial bracket for 25,000+ sq ft also falls to $0.05–$0.10 per sq ft per visit, and routine restroom rates drift toward $15–$22.

Large floors also justify machine work that small suites cannot. A cordless compact auto-scrubber such as the Tennant i-mop Lite, with a 14.5-in cleaning path, 0.8-gal tank, and 500 RPM twin brushes, can scrub multi-stall restroom tile and recover dirty solution in one pass, replacing string mops that push contaminated water into grout lines. For grout lines and corners, the Oreck Commercial 550MC Orbiter, a 24 lb oscillating machine with a 13-in pad, scrubs tile without the torque that makes rotary machines hard to control in tight stalls. Outside the restroom, a Powr-Flite P202-3 20-inch 2000 RPM burnisher with dust control keeps the adjoining VCT corridors from looking dull next to freshly scrubbed restroom floors.

blocks.title: Do not chase the low end blindly
blocks.text: Large-building bids below $15 per restroom per visit usually reflect understaffed routes. Check the implied labor: 0.15 to 0.25 hours per restroom per visit is the realistic floor for partitions, fixtures, dispensers, and floors.
Choosing the Right Contract Structure for Your Size

items.name: Count fixtures, not just restrooms
items.text: Pricing scales with fixtures. A single-user restroom and a 7-fixture core restroom should never carry the same per-visit price.

items.name: Identify your minimum threshold
items.text: If your descaling labor is under two hours, you will pay the minimum. Bundle or reduce frequency.

items.name: Request production assumptions
items.text: Large buildings should ask bidders to state fixtures per hour so you can audit the labor math.

items.name: Compare annual cost per fixture
items.text: Divide total annual restroom spend by fixture count to benchmark against similar buildings.

faqs.q: Why does my small office pay more per restroom than a large building?
faqs.a: Fixed costs such as travel, chemical setup, and PPE are spread over fewer fixtures. Most vendors also apply a $90–$135 per-visit minimum for routine service and a $110–$190 project minimum for descaling, which overrides per-fixture math in suites under 2,500 sq ft.

faqs.q: At what size do restroom economies of scale kick in?
faqs.a: The break usually comes when descaling labor exceeds two technician hours, roughly 8 to 10 fixtures. Beyond about 25 fixtures, crews can run continuous production routes and per-fixture costs fall into the $14–$24 range.

faqs.q: Should large buildings require a dedicated day porter for restrooms?
faqs.a: Buildings with more than 150 occupants or public-facing lobbies often add a day porter for midday restroom checks and restocking. Porter labor is typically billed at $35–$65 per hour and reduces complaints more than adding extra night visits.

faqs.q: Do safety requirements differ between small and large restroom programs?
faqs.a: The OSHA HazCom and Bloodborne Pathogens obligations are the same, but large programs involve more chemical volume, so ask for written dilution control, SDS binders on each floor, and a certificate of insurance with workers' compensation for every crew member.
